Agree means to be of the same mind as someone, or to say yes to something. Think of it as two things coming together and fitting — two opinions matching, two people accepting the same idea, or two facts lining up.

1. To Share the Same Opinion

This is the most common use. When you agree with someone, your view matches theirs. You think the same thing.

  • "I agree with you — this plan is risky."
  • "Do you agree that honesty is important?"
  • "She agreed with everything he said."

The opposite is disagree — when your opinion does not match.

Notice: you agree with a person, and you agree with a statement or opinion.

2. To Say Yes — To Consent or Accept

When someone proposes something (a plan, a request, an offer, a deal), and you say yes to it, you agree to it.

  • "He agreed to the terms of the contract."
  • "She agreed to help me move."
  • "They agreed to a ceasefire."

Here, "agree" means accepting something that was put in front of you. You are not just sharing an opinion — you are giving your approval or consent.

Notice the pattern: agree to + something or agree to + do something.

3. To Reach a Joint Decision Together

When two or more people discuss something and come to a common decision — not just one person accepting the other's idea, but both arriving at something together — they agree on it.

  • "We agreed on a meeting time."
  • "The two countries agreed on a trade deal."
  • "Can we all agree on what to order?"

The key difference between this and the previous meaning:

  • agree to → you accept something already proposed.
  • agree on → you and others figure something out together and both/all arrive at it.

4. To Be Consistent — When Things Match

"Agree" is also used when talking about facts, numbers, stories, or reports that are consistent with each other — when they line up and do not contradict each other.

  • "Your answer agrees with mine."
  • "The two witnesses' accounts do not agree."
  • "The lab results agree with what the doctor expected."

Here, the subject is not a person — it's a thing (a result, a statement, a figure). It simply means: these things are in harmony, they match, they are consistent.

5. To Suit Someone's Body or Health

This is a special use. When food, a climate, medicine, or a lifestyle suits your body — when it makes you feel well — we say it agrees with you. When it makes you feel unwell, it does not agree with you.

  • "Spicy food doesn't agree with me." (It upsets my stomach.)
  • "The cold climate didn't agree with her." (She fell ill or felt unwell.)
  • "Some medicines don't agree with everyone."

This use is always in the pattern: agree with someone/something, and it almost always appears in the negative.

6. Grammar: When a Word "Agrees" With Another

In grammar, we say a verb or adjective agrees with a noun when they correctly match in number (singular/plural), gender, or case — depending on the language.

  • "In English, the verb must agree with the subject in number: 'He runs' not 'He run.'"
  • "In French, adjectives agree with the nouns they describe."

This is a technical grammar term, but it follows the same logic: two things matching each other.
Key Preposition Patterns — All in One Place

Getting the preposition right is crucial. Here is how it works:

agree with someone → you share their opinion
"I agree with the professor."

agree with something → it matches, it corresponds, it suits
"This data agrees with our hypothesis."
"Dairy doesn't agree with him."

agree to something → you accept/consent to a proposal or request
"She agreed to the conditions."

agree to do something → you consent to perform an action
"He agreed to pay the fine."

agree on something → two or more people reach a mutual decision
"We agreed on a solution."

agree about something → two or more people share a view regarding a topic
"We don't always agree about money."

agree that + clause → you and others share a stated view
"They agreed that the situation was serious."
Agree — With No Object at All

Sometimes "agree" is used without any object. This simply signals that a consensus exists or is reached.

  • "Everyone agreed."
  • "We discussed it for an hour and finally agreed."
  • "I couldn't agree more." (a strong way of saying: I completely agree)

"I agree with you" vs. "I agree to it"

  • Agree with (a person or idea) = your opinion matches.
  • Agree to (a plan, request, or action) = you give your consent.

You would not normally say "I agree to you" — that sounds wrong because you agree to plans, not to people.

"Agree" does not always mean you are happy

You can agree to something even if you are not thrilled about it. It simply means you said yes.

  • "He reluctantly agreed to the new terms."

"Agree" implies two sides — at least implicitly

Even when only one person is mentioned, "agree" always implies there is another side — another person, a stated plan, an existing view, or an observable fact. You always agree with or to something. You never agree in isolation.

"I couldn't agree more" — strong agreement; you completely agree.

"We beg to disagree" — formal way of saying: we respectfully do not agree.

"Agree to disagree" — when two people accept that they will never share the same view on a topic and decide to leave it there.
"We've been arguing about this for years. Let's just agree to disagree."

"It was agreed that..." — passive form, formal; means all parties came to this conclusion.
"It was agreed that the project would begin in January."
